title: SYSK Selects: Scooby Dooby Doo, Where Are You?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode on Scooby-Doo, Where Are You? Chuck introduces it as a Saturday pick. The hosts cover the show's cultural staying power and a study where kids chose food from boxes with cartoon characters, including Scooby-Doo. They trace the development history: the early concepts Who's Scared? and Mysteries Five, the Mystery Inc. characters (based partly on the Archie gang and I Love a Mystery), the dog added at Fred Silverman's request, and how the name Scooby Doo came about. They discuss the non-violent format, the characters and their voice actors, the Hanna-Barbera limited animation technique, and the rumors (Shaggy and Scooby as stoners, Velma's sexuality, the Boston college myth). They also cover later incarnations and spin-offs such as Scrappy-Doo, Scooby-Dum, the hour-long movies with guest stars, and the Mystery Incorporated and Matthew Lillard versions. The episode ends with listener mail about a surgery mix-up.

segments.title: Intro and Scooby-Doo's staying power
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the episode as a Saturday Select pick. The hosts riff on the show's many versions, including a Russian version of the theme, and a study in which kids chose food from boxes with cartoon characters such as Scooby-Doo. They discuss why the show has endured, and compare it to Nancy Drew, the Hardy Boys, and Encyclopedia Brown.
topics: cartoon characters and children's food choices

segments.title: Development history and early concepts
segments.summary: The hosts trace the show's origins: the early titles Who's Scared? and Mysteries Five, and the influence of the radio show I Love a Mystery. Early characters were based partly on the Archie gang. The dog came from a Great Dane idea, and the band concept included a dog that played bongos. Names changed as the characters were reworked.

segments.title: Fred Silverman, the name Scooby-Doo, and the non-violent format
segments.summary: Fred Silverman, an ABC/CBS executive who wanted a half-hour show and loved dogs, shaped the series. Writers Joe Ruby and Ken Spears added the dog. The name is said to come from a Sinatra song. The show avoided violence in response to parent and church group pressure, so the characters outwit villains with traps.

segments.title: Premiere and the skeptical Mystery Inc. approach
segments.summary: The first episode, What a Night for a Night, aired in September 1969. The hosts describe the show's skeptical premise, in which ghosts are always revealed as humans. Fred is the skeptical leader, and the hosts describe his dapper look and cravat.
topics: What a Night for a Night

segments.title: Characters and voice actors
segments.summary: The hosts profile the gang. Fred is the leader, Velma is the smart, bookish one, and Daphne is often captured. Shaggy and Scooby are the hungry duo. The hosts name the voice actors for each character, including Don Messick, who also voiced Astro, and discuss Daphne's wealth and the Mystery Machine. Catchphrases such as jinkies and zoinks are mentioned.

segments.title: Stoner rumors and other fan theories
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the long-running rumor that Shaggy and Scooby were stoners and the denials from creators, including Iwao Takamoto. They also cover rumors about Velma's sexuality, Fred and Daphne as a couple, and the hosts' own childhood impressions.

segments.title: Later incarnations and side characters
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the hour-long movies with guest stars such as Don Knotts, Phyllis Diller, and the Harlem Globetrotters. They cover Scrappy-Doo, Scooby's nephew, who many fans dislike, and Daws Butler's Scooby-Dum. They also mention Butler's other voice roles and Hanna-Barbera's catalog, and the Teen Wolf cartoon.

segments.title: Limited animation and production process
segments.summary: Hanna-Barbera's limited animation method reduced cost by animating only moving body parts on separate cels, which explains Shaggy's still upper body. Takamoto avoided muzzle lines for more expressive faces. The hosts describe the production steps, from scripting and voice recording to overseas animation and digital coloring, and the roughly six-month timeline for a half-hour show.

segments.title: Myths, trivia, and closing remarks
segments.summary: The hosts cover the myth that the characters were based on five Boston-area colleges, which Hampshire College's later founding disproves. They close with the Mental Floss quiz, the Google Halloween logos, and the show's longevity.

segments.title: Listener mail: surgery mix-up
segments.summary: A listener relays a story from a friend of a friend about a wrong-side surgery mix-up. A nurse marked the wrong leg and both testicles were removed. This follows the hosts' earlier call for surgery horror stories on the acupuncture episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck thank listeners, mention social media and email, and sign off.
